 UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
 
 
 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 
et al.  
) 
Docket No. EL25-49-000  
Large Loads Co-Located at 
Generating Facilities

Docket No. AD24-11-000  
Constellation Energy 
Generation, LLC  
v.  
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.

Docket No. EL25-20-000  
(consolidated)  
 
 
COMMENTS OF THE EDISON ELECTRIC INSTITUTE  
 
 
 
Pursuant to Rules 206 and 213 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal 
Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC” or “Commission”),1 the Edison Electric Institute 
(“EEI”) respectfully submits the following comments in response to FERC’s order issued on 
February 20, 2025 (“Show Cause Order”) instituting this proceeding under section 206 of the 
Federal Power Act (“FPA”)2 and consolidating it with other proceedings.3  In the Show Cause 
Order, the Commission found that PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s (“PJM”) Tariff appears to be 
unjust, unreasonable, unduly discriminatory or preferential with respect to its treatment of issues 
related to large loads co-located at generating facilities.  FERC directed PJM and the 
transmission owners of PJM (“PJM TOs”) to either: (1) show cause as to why the PJM Tariff 
remains just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential without provisions 
addressing with sufficient clarity or consistency the rates, terms, and conditions of service that 
 
1 18 C.F.R. § 385.206 (2012); see also 18 C.F.R. § 385.213 (2012). 
2 16 U.S.C. § 824e (2006). 
3 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 190 FERC ¶ 61,115 (2025) (“Show Cause Order”).

2 
 
apply to co-location arrangements; or (2) explain what changes to the PJM Tariff would remedy 
the identified concerns if the Commission were to determine that the PJM Tariff has in fact 
become unjust and unreasonable or unduly discriminatory or preferential and, therefore, 
proceeds to establish a replacement PJM Tariff.  PJM, a group of indicated PJM TOs, and Public 
Service Electric and Gas Company (PSE&G) filed responses to the Show Cause Order on March 
24, 2025. 
 
EEI is the association that represents all investor-owned electric companies in the United 
States.  EEI members provide electricity for nearly 250 million Americans and operate in all 50 
states and the District of Columbia.  The electric power industry supports more than seven 
million jobs in communities across the United States.  EEI’s member companies own and 
operate generation, transmission, and distribution facilities in regions all throughout the country.  
EEI members are focused on keeping customer bills as low as possible, and these generation, 
transmission, and distribution facilities are helping to meet rising demand while creating good-
paying jobs and a cleaner, resilient, and affordable energy future for the customers and 
communities they serve.  Accordingly, EEI can provide a broad-based perspective on the issues 
raised in the Show Cause Order. 
I. 
BACKGROUND 
The electric grid has long provided an extraordinary platform to reliably and affordably 
serve the nation’s electric customers.  Among other things, the electric grid supports and 
facilitates the deployment of resilient, reliable sources of power, at scale, to address customers’ 
needs.  After an extended period of relatively low demand growth rates, the country’s electric 
sector has entered an era of rapid transformation and unprecedented and sustained load growth.  
The North American Electric Reliability Corporation (“NERC”), among others, has observed

3 
 
that load and demand on the nation’s electric system will continue to increase as a result of many 
factors, including growing digitization and electrification, as well as the “changing resource mix 
and increased reliance on variable resources and natural gas.”4  The Commission, in its most 
recent State of the Markets Report, stated that “[r]egions continue to confront challenges in 
assuring resource adequacy – challenges caused by extreme weather events, a changing resource 
mix, and shifts in load profiles.”5  The report also noted that most RTO/ISO peak demand 
forecasts have shown a trend towards faster load growth in recent years, shifting from prior 
projections of flattening or declining growth to projections of increasing growth.  A key facet of 
this growth in many regions is the emergence of new large load additions (e.g., from data 
centers).  Growth from this segment of the power sector is forecast to persist well into the future, 
and many regions are likely to see increases in large new loads seeking to connect to the electric 
system over the next several years.  For example, a recent Lawrence Berkeley National 
Laboratory report estimated that data center load growth tripled over the past decade and is 
projected to double or triple by 2028.6  A 2024 report by the Electric Power Research Institute 
(EPRI) projected that data centers will grow to consume up to 9.1 percent of U.S. electricity 
generation annually by 2030, compared to an estimated 4 percent today.7  At the same time, the 
electric industry is in the midst of a transformation, both in terms of the generation mix serving 
customers and customer makeup.  The electric system resource mix is evolving rapidly.   
 
4 See Statement of North American Electric Reliability Corporation, Technical Conference on Large Loads Co-
located at Generating Facilities, Docket No. AD24-11-000 (Nov. 1, 2024), at 2-3. 
5 See Fed. Energy Reg. Comm’n, 2024 State of the Markets Staff Report (March 20, 2025) at 8, 
https://www.ferc.gov/news-events/news/SMR-2024.  
 
6 Dep’t of Energy, DOE Releases New Report Evaluating Increase in Electricity Demand from Data Centers (Dec. 
20, 2024), https://www.energy.gov/articles/doe-releases-new-report-evaluating-increase-electricity-demand-data-
centers.  
7 Elec. Power Research Inst., Powering Intelligence: Analyzing Artificial Intelligence and Data Center Energy 
Consumption(May 2024) at 2, https://www.epri.com/research/products/3002028905.

4 
 
Ensuring that the nation’s electric companies can accommodate these generational 
changes and continue to serve customers in a reliable and affordable manner will require new 
and upgraded energy infrastructure at all points on the electric value chain: generation, 
transmission, and distribution.  Electric companies stand ready to lead the expansion of energy 
infrastructure needed to accommodate these changes.  The regulatory model that underlies the 
electric sector is, and will be, critical to meet this extraordinary period of new growth.  It ensures 
collaboration and partnerships between electric companies, stakeholders, and customers.  
Moreover, it serves as the foundation that supports the financing and construction of long-lived 
infrastructure.   
Against this backdrop, EEI submits the following general comments for the 
Commission’s consideration.  In doing so, EEI asks that the Commission ensure any action or 
decision in this proceeding does not adversely affect other regions and/or impede the ability of 
those regions to address any similar challenges in ways they believe to be just and reasonable. 
II. 
COMMENTS 
a. Electric companies stand ready to lead energy infrastructure 
expansion. 
Electric companies are best positioned to lead the expansion of energy infrastructure 
driven by the dynamics previously described.  This year, EEI members will invest $200 billion to 
make the energy grid smarter, more dynamic, more flexible, and more secure; to diversify the 
nation’s energy mix; and to integrate new technologies that benefit customers.  Electric 
companies have extensive knowledge of the electric system, deep, collaborative relationships 
with states and stakeholders, and, for decades, managed the development of infrastructure 
projects that take years to design, finance, and build.  Each of these capabilities is essential in 
assuring efficient, cost-effective, and timely infrastructure additions.  Moreover, experience in

5 
 
the recent past demonstrates that electric companies are capable of meeting new demand from 
large loads, including data center-based demand.  There is a data center located in every state in 
the country, and each project required careful planning before going into service.   
Electric companies have direct experience with the effects of rapid growth of large loads 
in their service territories.  Working in partnership with their states, these companies successfully 
accommodated that growth over time.  Electric companies have also announced numerous 
agreements and partnerships to facilitate data center development.  For example, northern 
Virginia, Dominion’s service territory, boasts the largest data center market in the world, and 
Dominion serves more data centers today than the next five largest national data center markets 
combined.8  In addition, AEP anticipates 20 gigawatts in new load by the end of the decade.9  
Exelon serves 200 online data centers in its service territories and projects significant continued 
load growth from data centers.10  States have also actively worked to prepare for load growth 
from large customers.  In January, the Georgia Public Service Commission voted unanimously to 
approve new rules that allows for longer contract lengths between and minimum billing 
requirements for high-load customers.11   
       
 
 
 
8 Comments of Dominion Energy Services, Docket No. AD24-11-000 (Dec. 9, 2024), at 2. 
9 Am. Elec. Power, AEP Reports 2024 Earnings Results (Feb. 13, 2025), 
https://www.aep.com/news/stories/view/10018/.  
 
10 Exelon, 2024 Earnings Call Presentation Slides (Feb. 12, 2025), https://investors.exeloncorp.com/events/event-
details/q4-2024-exelon-corporation-earnings-conference-call.  
 
11 GA Pub. Serv. Comm’n, PSC Approves Rule to Allow New Power Usage Terms for Data Centers (Jan. 23, 2025), 
https://psc.ga.gov/site/assets/files/8617/media_advisory_data_centers_rule_1-23-2025.pdf.

6 
 
b. The existing regulatory model can accommodate significant demand 
growth. 
The regulatory model that governs the electric sector is long-standing, well-understood 
and provides transparent processes that ensure prudent investment to serve customers.  This 
model successfully accommodated significant demand growth at different periods in the nation’s 
history and can continue to do so in the current environment.  In addition, this model provides 
stability and facilitates valuable partnerships between electric companies, regulators, 
stakeholders, and customers.  It will be a critical supporting element in meeting this 
extraordinary period of new demand growth.  Further, this regulatory model has been carefully 
developed over more than one hundred years and, as a result, electric companies, customers, and 
regulators have long-established approaches for working collaboratively to plan the supply 
additions and system expansions required to serve customers.  When they function properly, 
these approaches foster collaboration that ensures the necessary investments are made, 
infrastructure is developed, and critical public services are provided. 
This regulatory model has, among other things, helped to build an electric system that 
evolves and modernizes as it integrates new supply resources and demand (e.g., data centers).  
This networked system captures economies of scale and allows electric companies to meet new 
demand efficiently and cost-effectively, as demonstrated by the reliable addition of thousands of 
data centers across the nation.  Indeed, as noted above, America’s electric companies have been 
at the forefront in partnering with new large loads, such as data centers, to enable timely 
interconnections to the grid.  These instances demonstrate electric companies’ ability to 
proactively plan and invest in transmission and generation infrastructure that can facilitate large 
load development while achieving broader benefits for existing customers and communities.

7 
 
As the Commission recognized in its February 20th order in this proceeding, there are 
many different co-location configurations. Co-location, depending on configuration, provides 
optionality to serve data centers and may support data center development necessary for 
economic development and national security.  This could include: 
• Access to an integrated network of supply resources that permit cost-efficient operations 
• Holistic and comprehensive system planning that identifies new grid infrastructure to 
ensure reliable delivery of power 
• Provision of black start and ancillary services 
• Cybersecurity and physical security measures and protections will all contribute benefits 
to co-located load that is connected to the electric system.  
 
c. Principles for the Commission to bear in mind as it evaluates next 
steps. 
As the Commission evaluates the comments it receives in response to the Show Cause 
Order and contemplates its next steps, EEI asks that it keep several key principles in mind.  First 
and foremost, the Commission should strive to ensure that reliable system operations and 
resource adequacy are maintained and enhanced over the long term.  At the same time, co-
location policies should be grounded in cost-causation principles, ensuring that data center 
customers pay just and reasonable rates for service they use and protecting existing customers 
from any potential undue and unfair shifts in costs.  The Commission should also respect the 
jurisdiction of state regulatory authorities and consider how collaboration with state 
commissions, and RTOs/ISOs where applicable, may be valuable in addressing specific co-
location arrangements.  Adherence to these principles will ensure that rules and regulations will 
enable electric companies to continue their long history of delivering reliable and affordable 
service to customers and meeting the new system demands in a cost-effective, efficient, and 
timely way.

8 
 
III. 
CONCLUSION 
EEI appreciates the opportunity to submit comments in this proceeding and urges the 
Commission to act in a manner consistent with the principles discussed herein. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Respectfully submitted,
